title: Inside Phey, Ladakh, Where Water Lords and Household Rotas Govern Shared Resources
description: At 3,180–3,186 metres, Phey shares scarce meltwater through household turns. A stone check, a water lord and livestock rules reveal Ladakh’s village governance.
author: Avantika Krishna
content:
Before dawn, a farmer in Phey may be waiting for a turn that belongs to a carefully watched village schedule. Water is not taken whenever someone needs it. Its flow is shared through rules, turns, and people tasked with ensuring nobody takes more than their share.
At 3,180 – 3,186 metres in Ladakh’s cold desert, this is how the community manages scarce resources through duties.
A water turn is a village responsibility
Phey lies west of Leh town. Its irrigation story begins beyond its fields. The village shares a stream with upstream Phyang. Winter snowfall and spring weather influence when meltwater arrives and how much reaches the channels. Springs also feed ponds that supply some fields, while upper fields rely more heavily on the stream arriving from Phyang. The water’s arrival is tied to the thaw, so a poor winter or cool spring can affect sowing and irrigation.
A study by Dorjey Angchok, Tsering Stobdan and Shashi B Singh, using 1981 village-directory data, gives Phey 33 households and 176 people. It records household-based water distribution, rather than a channel-based rota, because the settlement was relatively small. These are historical figures, not a current population count.
The chhur-pon, literally the “water lord”, coordinates irrigation. The supervisor knows which field gets water, when and in what order. In Phey, the role works alongside a rota for guarding the main water-control point.
Households take turns sending people to watch the main sluice, or yur-go, that controls the main channel. Two people from each household are selected in rotation to check for blockages, overflow, or damage. When water is scarce, some must keep watch at night.
The village devised a way to verify that guards reached the control point. Each person breaks a stone in two, leaves one half at the sluice and carries the other to the next person on duty. The next guard checks whether the two pieces fit, making the rota accountable without a written register.
Rules also extend beyond the village boundary. Under a customary agreement known as the bandabas, Phey’s share of stream water from Phyang is protected from late evening until early morning during periods of scarcity after 21 June. It is one example of the traditional water systems of India that combine infrastructure with community rules.
Who watches the cattle?
Water is not the only resource that needs protecting. During the growing season, livestock straying into cultivated fields can destroy crops. Across Ladakh, the lorapa traditionally monitors free-grazing animals and prevents them from entering fields. Research documents this role as a regional institution; it does not establish that every village, including Phey today, follows it unchanged.
An animal found grazing where it should not can be taken to a lora, an enclosed cattle pound or cattle jail. Its owner must pay the penalty set under community rules to get it back. This makes each household responsible for protecting a neighbour’s crops.
The lorapa is generally selected for the cropping season, with duties and penalties agreed by the community. The goba, or village head, oversees village affairs, resolves disputes and coordinates these roles. Together, they form a local system of checks and responsibilities rather than one office doing everything.
A system under pressure
These arrangements developed in a landscape where farming depends on short growing seasons, limited cultivable land, and water from snow and ice. The region’s wider water crisis makes fair access all the more consequential. Ladakh’s ice stupas and community-built artificial glaciers are other examples of adapting water storage and distribution to these constraints.
But customary governance is not frozen in time. Research published in 2023 and 2025 describes pressures on Ladakh’s agropastoral systems, including tourism, new livelihoods, changing livestock patterns, fencing, and the overlap between traditional institutions and formal Panchayati Raj structures. The goba’s authority has weakened in some places, while fewer people may be available for seasonal duties such as the lorapa’s.
It depends on people continuing to participate, accepting shared rules and trusting others to do their turn. In Phey, even the stone-checking method shows how cooperation is reinforced by practical ways to discourage shortcuts.
A government outreach camp in Phey in November 2025 also recorded residents raising concerns about water scarcity, roads, school facilities and connectivity. Traditional institutions do not replace public services or remove the need for investment. They show how a village can organise the resources and responsibilities closest to home.
At this altitude, the rota is more than a timetable: shared resources depend on people keeping their word.

title: Uttarakhand Forest Fires: How Women Are Leading Community Forest Protection
description: Women in Uttarakhand are leading community forest restoration and fire prevention as migration reshapes Himalayan villages. Discover how initiatives in Manar and other villages are protecting forests and livelihoods.
author: Sriroopa Dutta
content:
Every morning, 75-year-old Bhagirathi Devi walks into the forest beside her village in Uttarakhand's Champawat district. She patrols the area, returns home around noon and heads back for another round at 2 pm, often staying until sunset.
Her task is to ensure that nobody cuts trees, damages vegetation or allows cattle to graze where they should not.
For more than two decades, Bhagirathi has helped protect and restore this forest in Manar village. Known locally as Van Amma, she began the effort in 2000, when the woodland had become almost barren following years of excessive grazing and tree felling.
Today, the community-managed forest is also a site of fire prevention.
In a report published by Down To Earth on 31 May 2025, journalist Bhagirath documented how the village's women organised themselves to restore the forest, regulate access, and remove dry leaves and pine needles before the fire season.
According to residents, there has been no forest fire in the restored forest since the initiative began. The Champawat Forest Department has also recognised the effort as a model for fire prevention.
Manar's experience points to something important about forest protection in Uttarakhand: preventing fires is not always about reaching a burning hillside with firefighting equipment. It can begin much earlier, with people who understand the forest, depend on it and have the authority to regulate how it is used.
Across the state's mountain villages, women are increasingly taking on this responsibility.
As men migrate in search of employment, women remain to manage agriculture, livestock and household needs. Their daily work brings them into close contact with forests, making them among the first to notice smoke and respond to small fires.
The Ghost Village question: who is left to protect the forest?
Uttarakhand's migration story is often told through the image of the ghost village: a settlement where houses remain locked, agricultural fields lie fallow, and only a handful of residents remain.
The scale of depopulation is reflected in government figures cited in the 2021 report Locked Houses, Fallow Lands: Climate Change and Migration in Uttarakhand, India, prepared by The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) and the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research.
According to the 2011 Census, 1,048 of Uttarakhand's 16,793 revenue villages were uninhabited. A subsequent survey by the state's Rural Development and Migration Commission in 2018 identified another 734 villages that had become uninhabited after 2011.
The report notes that depopulation has affected all 13 districts, although the problem is more pronounced in the hill districts.
However, not every village affected by migration is entirely deserted. In many settlements, men have moved to towns and cities for work while women, children and older residents remain. Women continue cultivating fields, looking after cattle, collecting forest produce and caring for family members.
This changes who is available to respond when a forest fire breaks out.
In Manar, Bhagirathi Devi's initiative began with a problem familiar to many women in mountain villages. Before the forest was restored, women had to walk seven to eight kilometres to a neighbouring forest, Siddhmandir, to collect fodder and firewood. Bhagirathi told Down To Earth that this journey took five to six hours every day.
The loss of nearby forest cover had also affected the flow of local springs. Restoring the woodland was therefore not simply a conservation exercise. It was an attempt to make village life more sustainable.
For women who remain, the responsibility is consequently twofold: maintaining households in villages with fewer working-age residents and protecting the natural resources that make those settlements habitable.
Why women are often the first to notice a fire
The reasons women become first responders are closely connected to the division of labour in rural households.
Collecting firewood and fodder, taking cattle to graze, gathering leaves and working on agricultural land are routine responsibilities for many women in Uttarakhand. These activities keep them in and around forests for several hours a day.
When a fire begins, they may notice the first signs of smoke before it becomes visible from the village or reaches the attention of forest officials.
A 2023 paper by researchers Ripu Daman Singh, Surabhi Gumber, R C Sundriyal, Jeet Ram and Surendra P Singh, published in Tropical Ecology, provides important context for understanding this relationship.
Titled Chir pine forest and pre-monsoon drought determine spatial and temporal patterns of forest fires in Uttarakhand Himalaya, the research analysed satellite-derived fire data from 2002 to 2020 across 24 forest divisions in the state.
The researchers recorded 80,440 fire detections over the 19 years. Their analysis found that warmer pre-monsoon temperatures, a greater proportion of chir pine forest and lower winter and pre-monsoon rainfall together explained 56% of the variation in fire incidence.
They also noted that human activities associated with farming and the collection of fuel and fodder influence the likelihood of fires.
The paper specifically recommends examining changes in population distribution and communities' dependence on forests as part of effective fire management.
This is where women's everyday relationship with forests becomes relevant.
They are not simply residents living near a fire-prone landscape. Their livelihoods are directly connected to the condition of that landscape.
A fire can mean losing fodder for cattle, travelling farther to collect fuelwood, spending additional hours searching for forest produce and, in some cases, losing agricultural resources.
The relationship between gender and firefighting is not simply a question of who is more willing to respond. It is also a question of who is expected to undertake the work when the forest that sustains the household is threatened.
In a report published by Mongabay on 8 September 2026, journalist Swati Thapa documented this pattern in Uttarakhand villages.
Researcher Kavya Pandey of the Centre for Wildlife Studies, Bengaluru, told Thapa that traditional gender roles and women's responsibility for household work and caregiving help explain why they are often the first to respond to fires.
This offers a field-level account of a wider connection between women's labour and forest protection.
How a community can stop a fire before it spreads
Manar offers a particularly useful example of what happens when women move beyond responding to individual fires and take responsibility for managing an entire forest.
When Bhagirathi Devi began the initiative in 2000, she brought other women together to form a van panchayat, a community forest-management council. She was unanimously elected its first sarpanch.
The initial work involved clearing and fencing parts of the degraded forest. The women also worked with BAIF Development Research Foundation, a Pune-based organisation involved in silvopasture initiatives in the region.
Silvopasture combines trees, grasses and livestock management. The idea was to restore vegetation while ensuring that the community could continue to access fodder and other forest resources.
With BAIF's support and training, residents fenced the woodland using stones and thorny plants. They cleared invasive species such as lantana and planted native trees and fodder species, including banj oak (Quercus leucotrichophora), angu (Fraxinus micrantha) and utish (Alnus nepalensis).
For two years, grazing was prohibited to allow the vegetation to recover. It took another five to six years for the trees to establish themselves.
According to Manju Manral, the first president of Manar's Silvopasture Management Committee, 11.6 hectares of forest were eventually revived.
The work was not entirely voluntary.
Down To Earth reported that women involved in the restoration received Rs 120 per day from BAIF. They voluntarily contributed 10% of their wages towards maintaining the forest. Each household also contributed Rs 20 a month towards Bhagirathi's salary for guarding the woodland.
A separate 2022 field study by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, BAIF and the Centre for Ecology Development and Research also found that the forest under Manar's van panchayat was healthier than the forest outside its management area.
What the 2026 fire season reveals
In an assessment published on 2 June 2026 on the Indian Institute of Remote Sensing's (IIRS) Sudoor Manthan science portal, researchers Athira V Mukundan, Madhusmita Murmu, Chandra Mohan Bhatt and Arijit Roy analysed forest-fire activity across the state between January and May 2026.
Using NASA's MODIS active-fire data, they recorded:
- January: 200 active-fire detections.
- February: 113 detections.
- March: 178 detections.
- April: 207 detections.
- May: 433 detections.
The May figure represented a 109% increase over April. It also accounted for approximately 38% of all detections recorded between January and May.
Pauri Garhwal recorded the highest cumulative number of detections during the five-month period, at 207, followed by Chamoli with 190 and Tehri Garhwal with 130.
The researchers also used Sentinel-2 satellite imagery to map burned areas in Pauri Garhwal. Comparing images from April with those captured between 25 and 28 May, they identified approximately 838.66 sq km of burned area. Most of this was classified as low-severity burning, while 0.94 sq km fell into the highest severity category.
These figures are satellite-based detections and mapped burn areas, not a count of independently verified individual fires. Nevertheless, they show how quickly fire activity intensified towards the end of the pre-monsoon season.
The 2023 research by Singh and his colleagues helps explain this seasonal pattern.
Most fires in Uttarakhand occur between March and May, when temperatures rise, vegetation dries and fresh pine litter accumulates on the forest floor.
The human cost of these fires can be severe. On 13 June 2024, four forest department personnel died while fighting a blaze in Binsar Wildlife Sanctuary in Almora district. According to a report by The Times of India on 14 June 2024, four others were seriously injured after the firefighting team was engulfed by flames.
For women who fight smaller fires in community forests, the risks are no less real, particularly when they have no protective clothing, footwear or firefighting equipment.
Besides, women's participation does not automatically translate into decision-making power.
A 2026 research chapter by K Nagahama, published in Springer Proceedings in Earth and Environmental Sciences, examines women's participation in a Uttarakhand van panchayat through household surveys, interviews, forest surveys and long-term observations conducted between 2011 and 2023.
The research examines an important distinction: being present in community forest management does not necessarily mean having equal authority over decisions or control over resources.
The problem is also visible in the reporting from Uttarakhand.
In her September 2026 Mongabay investigation, Swati Thapa spoke to Laxmi Kharayat, a field trainer with The Hunger Project, who described cases where women formally listed as van panchayat heads were unaware of their positions, while male family members exercised authority on their behalf.
There is also a gap between the work women undertake and the employment opportunities available to them.
Seasonal fire watchers recruited by the forest department are predominantly men. Women who assist in firefighting often do so without regular wages or access to appropriate protective equipment.
The Forest Fire Prevention and Management Scheme and India's National Action Plan on Forest Fires recognise the importance of early detection, community participation and coordinated firefighting. The challenge is to ensure that these provisions translate into practical support for women at the village level.
This means providing women with training in fire prevention and safe firefighting, protective clothing, gloves, sturdy footwear, communication equipment and access to emergency assistance.
It also means creating paid opportunities for women as seasonal fire watchers and ensuring that they have actual decision-making authority within van panchayats.
Just as importantly, their work should not be treated as an unpaid extension of household responsibilities simply because they are the people who remain in the village.
Forest protection begins with the people who depend on it
Bhagirathi Devi's work did not begin with a firefighting operation. It began with a forest that had become too degraded to support the people living beside it.
By bringing women together, restoring native vegetation, regulating grazing and establishing a system for removing dry litter, the village created a model of long-term community protection.
For women in Uttarakhand's mountain villages, protecting a forest also means protecting the resources that keep their households functioning.
When the forest burns, the consequences reach their cattle, farms, water sources and daily routines. Their leadership has shown that communities can play a significant role in preventing fires, provided they have the authority and resources to do so.
The next step is to ensure that this responsibility does not remain invisible or unpaid.
The women who recognise the first signs of smoke, organise their neighbours and maintain village forests should be treated as essential partners in forest protection, not as an informal firefighting force expected to manage with whatever tools they have at hand.

title: Watching a Press Wallah Discard Charcoal Inspired This Schoolgirl to Design a Solar Ironing Cart
description: For generations, India's neighbourhood press wallahs have relied on burning charcoal to earn a living. Watching one of them dispose of burnt charcoal prompted Tamil Nadu schoolgirl Vinisha Umashankar to explore an alternative.
author: Vaishali Gautam
content:
From school uniforms to office shirts, many of us rely on our neighbourhood press wallahs for freshly ironed clothes. The history of the tool they use goes back over 2,000 years, long before electricity entered our homes.
As early as the first century BC, people in China used metal pans filled with hot charcoal to remove creases from fabric. These heated pans were moved over stretched cloth to smooth out wrinkles.
In medieval Europe, blacksmiths made heavy, flat metal irons known as sadirons. These were heated over a fire or on a stove. Since they cooled down during use, people often kept several irons ready to use in rotation.
Charcoal irons offered another way to keep the metal base hot. Their hollow bodies held burning charcoal. In 1852, a patent was granted for a design featuring a chimney and ventilation openings.
In India, generations of dhobis, istriwallas and neighbourhood press wallahs have earned their livelihoods through washing and ironing clothes. Their work requires an understanding of different fabrics, heat and pressure.
The history of India's laundry trade is also linked to caste and hereditary occupations. For many families belonging to traditional washer communities, the skills involved in washing and ironing clothes have been passed down through generations.
In 1882, American inventor Henry W Seely patented an electric flat iron. His design used electricity to generate heat, eliminating the need to heat the iron over a fire or burn charcoal inside it.
Despite advances in ironing technology, charcoal irons remain a familiar sight on Indian streets. However, burning charcoal exposes vendors to smoke and contributes to air pollution. Producing charcoal can also contribute to deforestation.
At the age of 12, Vinisha Umashankar from Tiruvannamalai, Tamil Nadu, noticed an ironing vendor discarding burnt charcoal on her way home from school. She began researching its environmental impact and looking for a cleaner alternative.
Vinisha designed a mobile ironing cart that uses solar panels and batteries to power a steam iron. The cart could also accommodate mobile phone charging facilities, giving vendors another potential source of income.
The National Innovation Foundation developed a prototype in 2019. Two years later, Vinisha became the youngest finalist for the inaugural Earthshot Prize and, at 15, addressed world leaders at COP26 in Glasgow.
For centuries, people have found different ways to heat irons and remove creases from clothes. Vinisha's invention explores how an everyday service that supports generations of Indian families could become less dependent on charcoal.

title: Nvidia Reinstates Huang as AI Industry Faces Leadership Risks
description: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after a boardroom reversal backed by Donald Trump, sending shares soaring and raising questions about corporate power.
author: Frontline News Desk
content:
Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as president and chief executive officer of the world’s chipmaker by market value, marking a reversal in the history of the company and driving the stock to its biggest rally in decades. Fewer than two weeks after Huang departed Nvidia under the shadow of scandal, he is reclaiming both titles, the board stated in an announcement on November 23. US President Donald Trump had lobbied for the reinstatement, and the board cited input from the government of the United States when issuing the statement.
“Thank you all for the second chance. I am going to be a better CEO the second time around,” Huang told employees at Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, California. Chairman Harvey C. Jones said in the statement, "The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.”
Huang’s return follows weeks of turmoil at Nvidia, whose technology underpins the boom in artificial intelligence. The board had ousted him earlier this month after revelations that he had engaged in affairs outside his marriage—one with a subordinate and another with a woman whom the government of the US has investigated for espionage on behalf of China.
Supporters both within and outside the company, however, regarded the 63-year-old executive as irreplaceable. Huang had transformed Nvidia from a supplier of graphics chips into an enterprise valued at more than $5 trillion, while travelling the globe to champion AI as a revolution in industry.
News of his reinstatement sparked a rally for Nvidia. Shares surged 31 per cent to $165.05 in New York, marking the company’s highest gain in a single day since May 2003. Prior to the rebound, the stock had declined by roughly a third over the course of the year, erasing about $1.5 trillion in value on the market.
Nvidia’s board stated that its investigation into reports concerning Huang will continue, while the executive faces scrutiny from Congress over both his conduct and the export of technology to China. Huang is scheduled to sit for an interview with three committees of the House on December 1 and to testify before the Senate Banking Committee two days later at a hearing on export controls of the US. The company is still under scrutiny from investigators, including at the FBI and on Capitol Hill.
No consultation
People familiar with the deliberations said the board acted without consulting interim CEO Colette Kress or other executives, following an intervention by Trump, who pressed directors to make the move. Huang had appealed to the board for his return—a bid backed by some employees and prominent figures in Silicon Valley—after directors initially rejected his overture. The reversal echoed events at OpenAI in 2023, when Sam Altman was ousted as CEO and reinstated within a week amid backlash from investors and staff; like Huang, Altman is regarded as central to the development of AI.
Huang ranks as Nvidia’s fifth-largest shareholder with a stake of roughly 3.6 per cent, though he holds no shares with voting privileges of the kind that grant founders such as Mark Zuckerberg of Meta Platforms and Elon Musk of SpaceX control over their companies.
The executive relies on a style of management that involves intervening in problems at Nvidia and overseeing roughly 60 reports, nearly all in roles within engineering, including specialists in memory chips, networking, and graphics and processors.
“A lot of companies’ organisation charts, they all look the same. And it doesn’t make any sense to me. The architecture of the ‌company should reflect the environment in which it exists,” Huang said on a podcast in March. Huang has involved himself in the operations of startups backed by Nvidia, assisting them in securing customers and joining fundraising calls to attract investors, according to founders, venture capitalists, and a former Nvidia employee.
Huang’s return stumped many, and US lawmakers from both the Democratic and Republican parties strongly objected to his reinstatement. But it also reinforced the idea that some tech CEOs were considered irreplaceable, a big risk for ‌a company critical to the AI industry.
Speaking at a press conference in Brooklyn on November 23, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said: “I do not think that working people across the country signed up for their pensions being tied to the question of Jensen Huang’s fidelity to his marriage, and yet, for many days, that had a massive impact.”
He added, “We’re speaking about a divorce settlement that has been rumoured to be around $81 billion. That would be the cost of providing universal child care for every 3- and 4-year-old in the United States of America for an entire year. And a lot of this just brings to mind what Justice Brandeis said quite some time ago, which is, "We can have democracy; we can have great wealth concentrated in the hands of a few; we cannot have both.”
Nvidia leads the market in manufacturing accelerators for artificial intelligence—the chips used to train and run AI models—making the company a beneficiary of spending on infrastructure for data centres. The US government restricts sales of these chips to China, and Nvidia’s ties to the country, alongside its compliance with export controls, have drawn scrutiny.
Late last year, following lobbying from Huang, Trump loosened controls on chips and permitted Nvidia to sell its H200 processor—now generations behind its Vera Rubin line—to China. Last week, Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, informed investors that the chipmaker would halt sales of licensed H200 products to the country.
The company will hire a new chief compliance officer, and the board recently formed a committee to oversee national security and export control matters, it said in a statement.
Tech firms soar
News of Huang’s return, released shortly after the opening bell on November 23, sparked a surge across equities, driving shares of Nvidia up by 31.5 per cent and adding more than $900 billion to the valuation of the company. Other firms on Wall Street also drew buying interest, lifting the Nasdaq by more than six per cent, the S&P 500 by 4.7 per cent, and the Dow by three percent.
Markets in Asia, which had opened the week with losses, followed that trajectory. Taipei led the region with a nine per cent gain as chipmakers TSMC and MediaTek each rose nearly 10 per cent. Seoul climbed more than six per cent on advances from SK Hynix and Samsung.
Tokyo closed nearly four per cent higher, propelled by jumps of 12.5 per cent in Advantest, 7.7 per cent in Tokyo Electron, and 10 per cent in Kioxia. Exchanges in Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Wellington, Bangkok, and Manila also posted gains, while Hong Kong slipped as technology firms in China lagged behind the rally.
China’s warning
Huang’s comeback—prompted by the intervention of Trump—drew caution from state media in China. Less than three hours after the board issued its announcement, the Global Times published a commentary urging China to “remain vigilant”.
The article said, “It is foreseeable that the malicious attempts to sow discord in China-US relations will not automatically disappear simply because Huang has been reinstated.” It added that the next round of “witch hunts” could include investigation letters, delays in export licences and congressional hearings.
(with inputs from agencies)

title: Can Congress Turn Anti-AAP Sentiment Into A Comeback in Punjab?
description: Punjab’s 2027 Assembly election could offer the Congress a path to revival as anti-incumbency against AAP grows and the Akali Dal and BJP struggle to regain ground.
author: Zaid Bin Shabir
content:
On November 4, Rahul Gandhi returned to Punjab, a State where the Congress party has historically known how to sway voters and win elections. Launching the campaign for the Punjab Assembly elections in Sangrur, an Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) stronghold, Rahul attacked the AAP’s record in government and argued that Punjab needed a government that worked for the State rather than being “run from Delhi”.
The rally came at a time when the Congress, the ruling party in only one northern State, Himachal Pradesh, is trying to add momentum to its national-level recovery with a win in a State that had once been its stronghold. Also, after improving its Lok Sabha tally from 44 seats in 2014 to 99 in 2024, the party has increasingly sought to project Rahul as a more assertive opposition leader, taking on the Modi government.
But in Punjab, Rahul’s pitch was not simply an extension of that national campaign. His appeal to sentiments around Punjab’s distinct political identity builds on an older Congress-Punjab relationship.
For much of its post-Independence history, the Congress remained one of the principal political forces in Punjab as its journey intertwined with some of the many consequential changes in the border State. The party’s fortunes declined elsewhere following the BJP’s Modi wave, which swept away many of the Congress’ traditional strongholds after 2014. Yet Punjab, which brought the Congress back to power as recently as 2017, managed to buck the trend.
But voters in this outlier State have always shown little preference for continuity, which often results in the incumbent ruling party’s ouster. This happened in 2022 when the AAP mopped up 92 of Punjab’s 117 Assembly seats. The Congress, with just 18 seats, was roundly defeated. The State’s voters had built a new consensus that created a third political front.
“In 2022, the AAP was the only party that came into the fray without any baggage from the past,” said Sikander Singh, head of Misal Baba Sawan Singh Attari Dharna Dal, a Nihang Sikh group. “The driving force, which persuaded us to vote for it, was the AAP’s Delhi governance model, which had seemingly brought some relief to people there.”
However, with the passage of time, the ground beneath the AAP’s feet shifted. In the 2024 Lok Sabha election, it won only 3 seats while the Congress bagged 7 of the State’s 13 parliamentary constituencies. Growing popular disenchantment with the AAP government, which started drawing criticism well before the general election, was perceived to be the cause of this reversal. From governance issues to religious matters, Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann’s government has repeatedly found itself cornered.
Two years after the 2024 election, the AAP is out of power in Delhi and faces strong anti-incumbency in Punjab. Many observers believe that the situation creates a window for the AAP’s political opponents. With the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) struggling to recover its lost credibility and the BJP yet to establish a strong political base, political observers believe Punjab might become the first State to witness a Congress resurgence.
‘Price of power’
The AAP came to power promising a break from the politics of the Congress, the SAD, and the BJP. But its track record on its poll promises is severely contested. “People had very high expectations of the AAP,” said Jagrup Singh Sekhon, former professor of political science at Guru Nanak Dev University, Amritsar. “They thought the problem of drugs, gangsterism, law and order, unemployment, and mounting fiscal and agrarian crises would be addressed. But the AAP did not live up to those expectations.”
Popular discontent has coalesced around the problem of drug addiction. The government campaign on the issue, “Yudh Nasheyan Virudh”, was launched with much fanfare but has not yielded the desired results. The ruling party is perceived to be responsible for the mess.
“As we would fight to save our crops, so now we fight to save our generations,” said Sikander Singh. “The AAP promised to end the drug menace. Instead, drugs have become more easily available. Drugs and the AAP have devoured Punjab.”
The political damage has also acquired a consequential religious dimension. The acting jathedar of the Akal Takht, the highest temporal authority of Sikhs, has declared Mann “Guru Dokhi” (betrayer of the Guru) and “Khalsa Panth Virodhi” (anti-Khalsa Panth).
The State government’s record has also been complicated by the increasingly visceral question of who controls the Punjab’s government. The AAP government has been accused of allowing the ruling party’s central leadership in Delhi to exercise an outsized influence over the State. The impression is that the State’s affairs are being dictated by people with little understanding of, or empathy for, Punjab and its people.
Jagtar Singh, a senior journalist based in Punjab, said: “Immediately after the AAP formed the government, the perception in Punjab was that it was being run by people from Delhi. It was an open secret. Punjabis don’t like Delhi dictating the State, but the interference level keeps rising.”
The extent of that disconnect became apparent when Bhagwant Mann vacated his Lok Sabha seat after becoming Chief Minister in 2022. Barely three months later, the AAP lost the Sangrur bypoll. “It showed that the party’s connection with the people began to take a hit from the very beginning,” Jagtar Singh said.
The AAP, fighting to hold on to its last fort, has attempted to make Mann its Punjab face. Another move has been to drop eight sitting legislators, including Agriculture Minister Gurmeet Singh Khudian, in the party’s second list of candidates for the Assembly election, announced on November 12. But the damage, many observers believe, may be hard to reverse.
Sekhon observed: “The damage is already done. Once the Punjab elections are over, I don’t see the AAP continuing as a national party. The AAP may become a marginalised party. That’s the price of power in Punjab.”
The revival bid
Punjab has five principal contenders heading into next year’s election. Each is fighting, in its own way, to recover the political ground it has lost.
The SAD, one of Punjab’s oldest parties, is struggling to reclaim the political space it once occupied almost by default. The Badals’ centralisation of the party weakened its electoral base. Further, its alliance with the BJP—whose centralised model sat uneasily with the SAD’s regional identity—eroded its credibility. By the time the Akalis walked out over the controversial farm laws, they had already ceded much of their Sikh identity or Panthic political space to splinter groups and neo-Panthic forces such as the Akali Dal Waris Punjab De.
The SAD was reduced to three Assembly seats in 2022 and one parliamentary seat in 2024. Other groups filled the vacuum with Waris Punjab De chief Amritpal Singh and independent candidate Sarabjeet Singh Khalsa winning two core SAD strongholds, Khadoor Sahib and Faridkot, in 2024. Sarabjeet Singh Khalsa’s father was one of the assassins of former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.
Sekhon said: “The BJP has nothing to lose. But if there is any restructuring of the seat-sharing arrangement then the [Shriomani] Akali Dal has a double challenge, and it is already marginalised. People still identify problems [of drugs, corruption, sacrilege, and gangster culture] with its leaders.”
He added: “This accumulation of baggage makes the SAD-BJP reunion as much a risk as a political opportunity.”
The radical political space also appears to be narrowing. “The era of Amritpal [style of politics] has passed,” Sekhon said. “There was a particular momentum in 2024, especially in rural, agrarian constituencies, where voters wanted to teach Arvind Kejriwal and Narendra Modi a lesson and Amritpal became a vehicle for that anger.” His Akali Dal (Waris Punjab De) later contested the Tarn Taran Assembly bypoll but lost.
The BJP has failed to build an independent electoral presence in Punjab, either in seats or in vote share, notwithstanding its 24-year alliance with the SAD. In other States, the BJP has created a record of starting out as a weaker ally to a strong regional party and gradually growing into the dominant force. The did not happen in Punjab.
Ashutosh Kumar, professor of political science at Panjab University, Chandigarh, argued in his study “The 2024 Parliamentary Elections and Punjab Politics: Commonalities, Exceptionalism, and Takeaways” (published in the Journal of Sikh & Punjāb Studies in 2024) that the BJP is likely to remain a force in Punjab despite its electoral setbacks. But its growth, he noted, will depend on whether it can move beyond cultural nationalism and religious mobilisation, take clearer positions on issues concerning Punjab and Sikhs, and shed its anti-farmer image. The party also needs stronger State-level leadership, he argued, as its national leaders have little traction in Punjab and leaders brought in from the Congress, including Captain Amarinder Singh, Sunil Jakhar, and Manpreet Badal, have failed to give it the political momentum it needs.
The Congress, unlike the SAD and the BJP, is not trying to build a new political base. Notwithstanding its crushing 2022 defeat, the party retained a State-wide organisation and a large social coalition. Its seven Lok Sabha seats in 2024 offered enough evidence that voters who abandoned the party in 2022 had not necessarily moved beyond it.
Kumar observed that the Congress has retained a cross-community base that can become electorally decisive if the AAP’s support continues to erode. According to him, the Congress managed to retain its old social base at a time when political loyalties were becoming fragmented in Punjab.
Sekhon explained why the Congress has an advantage: “Today, the AAP is no longer the outsider that promised to disrupt Punjab’s established political order. It is the incumbent defending its record. While others are caught in some major crisis or the other, the Congress has returned to being a principal challenger, its most comfortable role in Punjab.”
The Congress, meanwhile, has sought to contain factionalism by bringing in Sachin Pilot as Punjab in-charge and former Indian hockey team captain and three-time MLA Pargat Singh as State Congress president. “The combination has helped control the strife to a great extent,” Sekhon said.
Harjeshwar Pal Singh, a professor of history, also said that the Congress has a solid base in Punjab. “It has a presence in almost every district, every village, and every mohalla. It has leaders known across the State,” he said. “That is a strength which cannot be created overnight and other parties currently lack it.”
The Punjab edge
This will be the first State election in northern India since the Cockroach Janata Party(CJP) protests forced the Modi government to confront a series of political controversies. The agitation against the former Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan and then the protests over voter exclusions through the Special Intensive Revision have added to the political goodwill of Rahul Gandhi, as Leader of the Opposition in Parliament, and of the Congress as the major opposition party.
Uttar Pradesh, like Punjab, will also go to the polls next year. But in Uttar Pradesh, the Congress remains one among several political players. The BJP, the Samajwadi Party, and the Bahujan Samaj Party all have considerable influence in the Uttar Pradesh contest. Punjab is different.
Politics in Uttar Pradesh is influenced by politics at the national level. In contrast, Punjab has remained more immune to national developments. “Punjab has never been swayed by the ‘national constituency phenomenon’, attempted earlier by the Congress and now by the BJP, both polity wideparties,” Professor Ashutosh Kumar wrote in his 2024 study. “The latter’s repeated attempts to contest elections on national issues like national security, Article 370, citizenship, exalted status of India on the global stage, has not cut much ice in the State. On the contrary, even in the Lok Sabha elections, local issues like drugs, mafia hold, the farming sector distress, have remained decisive.”
He added: “At a time when there has been a growing perception about a large-scale ideological shift from middle to right-wing conservatism, visible in the ascendance of cultural nationalism in the plains and hills of north, central, and western India, Punjab again seems immune from it, despite having a sizeable Hindu population.”
That distinctiveness, in addition to Punjab’s social composition, has created a natural advantage for the Congress. Unlike other political parties, the Congress has usually drawn support across Sikh, Hindu, and Dalit constituencies.
“Punjab, along with Kerala, is a State that is most productive for the Congress because it is a catch-all party,” explained Harjeshwar Pal Singh. “It does not cater to one particular social group. It has historically brought different identities into the same political coalition.”
No room for complacence
The Congress may have emerged as the principal challenger to the AAP, but the voters who want the AAP out still have to decide which party they believe can replace it. This is where this election differs from the 2022 election, as Sekhon explained: “The 2022 election was altogether different. People had an option then that was relatively free of the political record of the established parties. This time, almost all the parties are sailing in the same waters. It’s not a vote for the best party but a choice of lesser evil.”
That difference could have implications for the Congress’ prospects.
“The biggest advantage of the Congress is that it does not have to convince Punjab to accept it as a political force,” said Harjeshwar Pal Singh. “The question is whether it can convince different social and religious groups that they have a common political interest in bringing the Congress back.”
The calculation could also become particularly important among Punjab’s floating voters who have repeatedly shifted their loyalties. “Punjab’s floating voter is not necessarily looking for the party with the strongest ideology,” said Sekhon. “She is looking at which party can actually form the government. Once the voter starts believing that one party has the capacity to win, the floating vote begins moving in that direction.”
That is where the Congress’ rise as the principal opposition becomes electorally significant. It makes the party a plausible choice for voters who want to punish the AAP but may not be entirely sure of whom they want to reward, said Sekhon.
Yet, there is no room for complacence. “The Congress cannot assume that every voter who is unhappy with the AAP will automatically come to it,” said Jagtar Singh. “Punjab has shown many times that people can reject one party without necessarily choosing the traditional alternative. The Congress has to make itself the obvious alternative. If the voter thinks there is uncertainty about the Congress, the anti-government vote can still be divided.”
There is also a limit to what Rahul Gandhi can do for the party. His confrontation with the Modi government and his association with the farmers’ cause have given the Congress an additional political resonance in Punjab. But the Assembly election will eventually be decided on questions of local relevance.
“Rahul Gandhi can create a political atmosphere, but the Punjab election will be fought by the State leadership,” said Harjeshwar Pal Singh. “People will ask who is going to run Punjab, what they will do about drugs, employment, farming, and law and order. The Congress has to give them an answer that is bigger than simply defeating the AAP.”
Indeed, an anti-incumbency vote many not be easy to consolidate. “People in Punjab defeat a party, they don’t elect a party,” said Jagtar Singh. “They can decide that a government has to go without having already decided which party should replace it.”
Zaid Bin Shabir is a journalist based in Srinagar.

title: O.P. Sharma: Remembering India's last pictorialist
description: Exploring the life, experiments and enduring legacy of O.P. Sharma.
author: Rahaab Allana
content:
The revelation, if it comes at all, will come in a small fraction of a second with an unconscious gesture, a gleam of the eye, a brief lifting of the mask that all humans wear to conceal their innermost selves from the world. In that fleeting interval of opportunity the photographer must act or lose his prize. —Yousuf Karsh
A woman emerging through the surface of a painting as if stepping out of a dream; a shipwreck that seems to etch a moment from W.H. Auden’s elegiac poetry; a black cat fixates on the viewer, apparition-like, in a graveyard, much like a frame lifted from a Murakami novella; angular shards of light create anthropomorphic forms at the Ellora caves; supernatural beams of light emanate from a portrait, like in a 1980s sci-fi film poster; as Bismillah Khan is lost in a rhapsodic trance, a musical instrument materialises like a mirage around him. Such is the ethereal image-making of O.P. Sharma, widely regarded as India’s last pictorialist. He passed away on November 6, at the age of 89, in Delhi.
Just a few weeks ago, while viewing “Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography” at the Tate Modern in London, I stood enraptured, once again, in front of a work by him from the 1960s. It was profoundly moving to see this master artisan, portraitist, and technical wizard in the company of some of the world’s greatest image-makers. The recognition was timely though long overdue—and yet it left me wanting more. More images and a suitable commendation.
My own deep interest in his oeuvre had been initiated through his 1998 solo exhibition catalogue, presented by Art Heritage gallery in Delhi, authored by the prolific critic of his time, K.B. Goel. Later, in 2010, pictorialism as a field became a disciplinary concern, while I was co-curating “The Artful Pose: Early Studio Photography in Mumbai (c. 1855–1940),” which included atmospheric images from the 19th and early 20th centuries, at the city’s Dr. Bhau Daji Lad Museum. And finally, in 2020, after persistent efforts, and some absurd coincidences (there was another younger artist of the same name at Triveni Kala Sangam whom I had mistakenly scheduled to meet), I was extremely privileged to have, finally and formally, encountered “O.P.” at his home in Bharati Artists’ Colony in Delhi’s trans-Yamuna area.
Interestingly, the colony came into being some decades after artists resettled in Delhi post-Partition; among them were B.C. Sanyal, Kanwal and Devayani Krishna, Dhanraj Bhagat, and P.N. Mago, who in 1949 founded the Delhi Silpi Chakra, a mutual-aid society and salon for artists (Satish Gujral and Richard Bartholomew would join it later). Born from a desire to retreat from the city centre, the colony paired homes with attached studios to give artists an ideal environment for creative productivity.
Nervously excited at the prospect of an engagement with the genius, I arrived for our meeting accompanied by my friend, Srinivas Kuruganti, former photo editor of TheCaravan. O.P. ji sat at one end of the living room, lamplight illuminating his profile; on the wall next to him was a garlanded photograph of his late wife/creative partner, Chitrangada, daughter of the very same noted modernist artists, Kanwal and Devyani Krishna. Surrounded by black-and-white prints, photo catalogues and books, he was peering intently at a newspaper article. He looked up at us from under those distinctive bushy eyebrows, smiled a welcome. Srinivas soon started filming. O.P. spoke about photography as the bedrock of his personal and professional life, ending almost every sentence with a mild ironic “samjhe?” (do you understand?) For many months, Srinivas and I contemplated whether he had endearingly named us “Sanjay”.
What attracted me most to O.P.’s thought and ethic was his unwavering conviction that photography as a craft and profession was most intensively developed by the passionate, dedicated, largely self-taught practitioner. As he remarked in a 2020 interview (to Diva Gujral), “Pictorial photography is the mother of all branches of photography”; and its biggest contributors are amateurs “who spend their time, money, energy and their life to discover new things”. And he was absolutely firm on how images should be “made”—not just “taken”—and developed: as analogue prints, with each frame pictorially conceptualised before the shot, and with desired effects created in the darkroom.
****
Over the years, it was clear that O.P. ji needed to be adequately recognised. And so, immersive discussions began in connection with the Alkazi Foundation’s planned tribute (in partnership with Art Heritage gallery) to his work at Shridharani Gallery in Delhi, in an exhibition titled “O.P. Sharma and the Fine Art of Photography: 1950s-1990s” (2024). This moment brought us—Sukanya Baskar (the assigned lead curator) and me (her collaborator)—into close contact with O.P. time and again, and to those nearest to him, his son and daughter-in-law, Aseem Sharma and Mohita Junnarkar, dedicated and loving caregivers.
After each session we were treated to delicious cutlets and samosas from a Nathu’s outlet in the neighbourhood. It was very rewarding to eventually open his show on Teacher’s Day, in the very same gallery which had hosted his first exhibition in 1963. O.P. eventually spent days at the exhibition, interacting with former students and conducting walkthroughs. We observed how he had touched the lives of so many in the city. They all came to pay their respects and absorb his astute observations on image-making.
Fascinating insights
Discussions with O.P. ji yielded fascinating insights. O.P.’s engagement with the medium began in 1954, inspired by the work of Armenian-Canadian photographer Yousuf Karsh (opening quote) at an international exhibition hosted by the UP Amateur Photographic Association in Lucknow. During his university studies there, a physics professor taught him to develop black-and-white film, triggering his lifelong obsession with the darkroom and technical experimentation; he gave up fine arts and committed himself to photography. “My interest grew, and eventually, my naani [maternal grandmother] presented me with a twin-lens reflex German camera but she also told me she could not spend any more money on this. Therefore, I used to walk from my home to the college, to save four annas to buy film and paper,” O.P. recalled in a 2018 interview. He learnt aspects of the craft from senior members of the Lucknow Camera Club.
Arriving in Delhi in 1958, O.P. ji joined Modern School as a teacher; he set up its photography unit and darkroom, and began a four-decade career during which he trained generations of students and furthered his own professional excellence. His future father-in-law, Kanwal Krishna, taught art at the school; its director, the prolific M.N. Kapur, himself an enthusiastic lensman, was an anchor. The Kapur daughters, Geeta (later a renowned art critic) and Anuradha (later a renowned theatre director) posed for O.P., who spent endless hours in his studio and the school darkroom, absorbed in technical experiments. Modern School is just down the road from Mandi House, Delhi’s hub of cultural venues where greats from every discipline—theatre, classical music and dance, literature, visual arts—regularly performed; concerts were also frequently held on the school campus. O.P. photographed many virtuosos on stage and invited them to his studio to sit for portraits—portraiture was a genre in which his skills found sublime expression.
O.P.’s Rasa Bhava Darshan project—an extended collaboration with the veteran Bombay theatre/film actor Sajjan Lal Purohit, completed in phases between 1960 and the mid-1970s— drew on Manmohan Ghosh’s translation of Bharat Muni’s Sanskrit treatise Natya Shastra to visualise the eight primary rasas and 49 bhavas of classical Indian aesthetics as a photographic portrait series. Working with scholar/dramaturge Brij Vallabh Mishra, Sajjan posed while O.P. photographed; the massive suite of images was entirely shot in the actor’s home.
A selection was exhibited between 1979 and 1980. In the exhibition brochure, O.P. described his use of Miranda and Asahi Pentax 35mm cameras, 500-watt photoflood lamps, and natural light to play with tonal values of grey; the images were finalised in a Kodak D-23 developer, and printed on Agfa-Gevaert paper. This stunning series was published as a book in 1998, and was meant to be rendered as a 25-minute film on 16 mm, incorporating paintings by Ram Kumar. It was through Sajjan that O.P. and Chitrangada found work in the Indian film industry; the couple created publicity stills for Do Boond Pani (1971); Siddhartha (1972); Chhupa Rustam (1973); and Shalimar (1978).
From 1980 onwards, O.P. ji and Chitrangada directed the Camera Art Institute at Triveni Kala Sangam, the holistic arts institution at Mandi House, conceptualised in 1950 by Sundari Shridharani and Uday Shankar. O.P. ji soon joined, and directed his pedagogy towards both theory and practice, especially printing and technical processes. Photographer Chandan Gomes, a former student, recalls “looking up in awe at a quiet, scholarly gentleman” with “immaculately combed hair, a gentle smile and a piercing gaze”, who “spoke with a calm certainty that made you listen to him with complete concentration” (“Remembering the Photographic Legacy of O.P. Sharma” by Chandan Gomes, published in Critical Collective on October 24, 2024).
Echoes of Surrealism
The restrained demeanour belied O.P.’s rigour; he was a perfectionist and formidable taskmaster, and those who could not grasp principles of optics to the required high level failed the course. Sifting one day through the papers in his studio with Sukanya Baskar, we found pages liberally marked in red ballpoint, with words and phrases enthusiastically circled and underlined.
Through the 1980s, he explored camera-less techniques of image production: controlling light or using chemicals to imprint photosensitive paper and create photograms, photomontages, sodium sulphite prints and collages. This radical experimentation echoed Western movements of the 1920s such as Surrealism and New Vision, and O.P. became known for his invention of what he called the “C-effect”, which produced distinct swirl patterns and infused the image with movement. He also wrote do-it-yourself instruction manuals in English and Hindi. And to O.P. goes the credit for having August 19—the day the French government officially announced the invention of the daguerreotype by chemist-artist Louis Daguerre in 1839—declared as World Photography Day in 1991. He had personally written to as many as 200 photographic societies, artists, and institutions around the world to gain support for this cause.
Along with technological innovation and teaching, and in alignment with his belief in his medium as a social and cultural good, O.P. devoted much time and energy to founding photography groups in different cities and promoting their work. These included the Amateur Photographic Society of Agra (1959), the Foto Arte Group (1974), and the India International Photographic Council (IIPC), established in 1983 and active to this day. The IIPC organised educational workshops, published a monthly journal, and created spaces for discussion, critique and documentation, thus ensuring custodianship of pictorialist legacies.
This last-mentioned endeavour acquired great significance in the context of the intense ongoing debate between Indian photographers and photojournalists about the primacy of genre: the value, necessity, and relevance of documentary realism versus those of pictorialism. Jury members of the First Indian Biennale of Photography, organised by the Lalit Kala Akademi in 1989, included O.P.’s close associate T. Kasinath, the then Director of the Photo Division of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, who actively pushed for the recognition of pictorial photography. However, submissions to the Second Indian Biennale of Creative Photography in 1993, in which O.P. participated, clearly indicated that despite methodological and thematic expansion, pictorialism as an aesthetic choice was now on the wane.
O.P. had long considered contemporary photography to be awash with misconceptions—about the digital era, about rules of composition, about the intricate analogue grammar now seemingly lost to point-and-shoot generations. “If a photograph is technically poor, it is only half a photograph. Unless you understand each and every part of the photographic process—from pressing the shutter to producing the final print—you can’t produce a good image,” he declared in a 2018 interview. Kodak founder George Eastman’s famous tagline, “You press the button, we do the rest”, was read by O.P. as an admission that many of us do nothing but mechanically press buttons.
The last few years have been special. I was honoured to guest-edit Aperture magazine’s Delhi issue in 2021, titled Looking Out, Looking In. The master’s dazzling, mesmeric portrait of Geeta Kapur, embodying both his technical virtuosity and creative philosophy, was selected by the Aperture editors for the cover. “A photograph on its own is like an uncut diamond,” he remarked as we reviewed captions for his 2024 tribute show. “Only when you understand every part of the photographic process—as Ansel Adams and Edward Weston did—and refine and polish the stone, does it become a Kohinoor!”
Rahaab Allana is Curator/Publisher, Alkazi Foundation for the Arts, New Delhi.
